summary.text: A man in his 70s with a pacemaker placed for 2:1 heart block and replaced a year earlier, glaucoma, hypertension and recurrent epididymitis, living with his spouse and owning a pet dog (yet described as having no interaction with farm or domesticated animals), had three months of cold and shivering episodes (rigors) two to three times a week with subsequent excessive heat and temperature rise to 38 degrees Celsius. There were no reported loss of consciousness, tongue biting, eye-rolling or incontinence episodes. He had received two courses of oral antibiotics from his general practitioner and then intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam on presentation.

On admission he was haemodynamically stable with no noteworthy examination findings and no signs of infective endocarditis or pacemaker pocket infection. On examination he had a fluctuating temperature with otherwise quite stable vital signs, normal heart sounds without murmurs or added sounds, a clear chest without consolidation, a soft lax abdomen without palpable organs and no cellulitis of the leg.

He was treated on admission for an infection of unknown origin. Workup showed leucocytosis with neutrophilia, fluctuating raised C-reactive protein, initially negative blood cultures, normal urine microscopy, negative urine nitrite, negative respiratory PCR for respiratory syncytial virus and COVID-19, a paced rhythm on ECG, negative infectious serologies, unremarkable chest X-rays and CT of thorax, abdomen and pelvis, and normal transthoracic echocardiography. After the intravenous antibiotics were discontinued, blood cultures grew coagulase-negative Staphylococcus epidermidis, and transoesophageal echocardiography showed echogenic shadowing of at least 2.5 by 1.3 cm on the right ventricular pacing lead with vegetation, consistent with a likely endocarditis of the ventricular pacing lead.

Treatment began with vancomycin and gentamicin; after sensitivity testing vancomycin was stopped and flucloxacillin and rifampicin were added with gentamicin continued. The infected pacemaker was surgically removed, a four-week course of vancomycin was given, follow-up blood culture was negative, and a new pacemaker was inserted. He was discharged safely, has remained asymptomatic since removal of the old pacemaker lead, and is due to be followed in the outpatient pacing clinic.
